newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA'S ANC SAYS PALME KILLERS MUST FACE JUSTICE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA'S ANC SAYS PALME KILLERS MUST FACE JUSTICE.

text.p: The former chief of a covert South African police hit squad said on Thursday an apartheid spy had been involved in the 1986 assassination of Swedish prime minister Olof Palme.
Eugene de Kock made the allegation while testifying in mitigation of sentence before the judge who convicted him last month of six murders and a series of other crimes.
President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) reacted to the disclosure on Thursday night saying that -- if true -- it owed it to Sweden to ensure the perpetrators faced justice.
De Kock, a colonel in the apartheid-era police, told the judge he had volunteered information to the prosecution.
"Like the assassination of Swedish prime minister Olof Palme," he said.
"It was one of Craig Williamson's 'Operation Long Reach' projects. I wanted it to be investigated before it was covered up," he said.
Williamson was one of the white minority government's most effective spies during the 1970s and 1980s and has admitted to carrying out bombings and other actions against anti-apartheid activists.
He could not be reached immediately for comment on de Kock's statement. Operation Long Reach was a secret programme by the apartheid government to harass or silence its opponents abroad.

The ANC, calling Palme a friend and staunch supporter of its anti-apartheid struggle, said it had requested the Attorney- General's office to keep a close watch on de Kock's trial to ensure that if international terrorism had been committed, legal action would be instituted.

"The people of South Africa owe it to Olof Palme and the people of Sweden, and democrats the world over, to ensure that the perpetrators of this evil deed face the full might of the law," the ANC said in its statement.
The former black liberation movement also called on ex-president F.W. de Klerk's white-led National Party (NP) to make public any knowledge it might have on Palme's death.
"The National Party government must come clean on their knowledge or otherwise of this matter.

"The ANC has always believed that the murder of anti- apartheid activists at home and abroad was not the work of maverick elements within the former security forces, but a cold and calculated state action against democrats the world over," the party said.
De Kock has previously said during the trial that he and Williamson collaborated in blowing up the ANC's offices in London while the ANC was still waging its liberation struggle.

He gave no indication what motive Williamson would have had for involvement in Palme's murder but the Swedish leader had close ties to the ANC, which took power in South Africa's first all-race election in 1994.
Palme's assassination by a gunman in a Stockholm street has never been solved although a broad range of theories have been put forward. The murder weapon has never been found.
De Kock has applied to the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission for amnesty for his crimes.
The commission, set up to heal the wounds of apartheid, has powers to grant amnesty to perpetrators of human rights abuses who confess to their deeds.
